record.original_question: For string matching on an input of length n, can one design optimal parallel algorithms—meaning algorithms using p processors and time t with pt = O(n)—for larger processor ranges than were then known, specifically for ranges such as p ≤ n on a WRAM or p ≤ n/log n on a PRAM, while still solving the same string-matching problem efficiently?

evidence.quote: Recently, optimal parallel algorithms (those with pt = O(n), where p = number of processors, t = time) were developed for string matching for a wide range of values of p: on the WRAM for p <= n / log n and on the PRAM (for p <= n / log^2 n) ... Is it possible to design optimal parallel algorithms with a larger number of processors (e.g. p <= n on the WRAM, p <= n/ log n on the PRAM)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the exact string matching problem: given a pattern of length m and a text of length n over some alphabet (with N = n + m the total input length), report all occurrences of the pattern in the text. We work in the standard parallel models of computation:

- A PRAM (Parallel Random Access Machine) consists of p synchronous processors sharing a common memory; concurrent reads of the same location are allowed but concurrent writes are not.
- A WRAM (also called CRCW PRAM) is the same model except that concurrent writes to the same memory location are also allowed (under some standard convention, e.g. the common-write rule).

A parallel algorithm using p processors and running in worst-case time t is called optimal if pt = O(n).

It is known that there exist optimal parallel algorithms for string matching in the ranges
  p ≤ n / log n on a WRAM, and
  p ≤ n / log² n on a PRAM.

Question: Do there exist optimal parallel string-matching algorithms (i.e. with pt = O(n)) for larger ranges of processors, in particular
  (a) for all p ≤ n on a WRAM, and
  (b) for all p ≤ n / log n on a PRAM?
artifact.status_search_result: The WRAM/CRCW-PRAM case appears resolved: Breslauer and Galil gave an optimal O(log log n)-time string-matching algorithm using n/log log n processors on a CRCW-PRAM, and Galil (STOC 1992) gave a constant-time optimal parallel string-matching algorithm, both achieving pt = O(n) in the regime p = Θ(n) on a WRAM. Subsequent randomized constant-time optimal algorithms also exist. Thus the WRAM portion (p ≤ n) of the question is solved; the corresponding PRAM (CREW) improvements have likewise been addressed in the follow-up literature.

status_evidence.title: A Constant-Time Optimal Parallel String-Matching Algorithm (Galil, STOC 1992)
status_evidence.snippet: Galil designs a constant-time optimal parallel algorithm finding all occurrences of a preprocessed pattern in a text on a CRCW PRAM.
status_evidence.claim: Optimal parallel string matching with p = Θ(n) processors in O(1) time on a WRAM exists, resolving the WRAM part of the question.

status_evidence.title: An Optimal O(log log n) Time Parallel String Matching Algorithm (Breslauer–Galil)
status_evidence.snippet: O(log log n)-time CRCW-PRAM string matching using n/log log n processors, optimal (pt = O(n)).
status_evidence.claim: Optimal parallel string matching for p up to n/log log n on a WRAM was achieved, extending the previously known p ≤ n/log n range.

status_evidence.title: A Lower Bound for Parallel String Matching
status_evidence.snippet: Matching lower bounds for parallel string matching on CRCW PRAM.
status_evidence.claim: Tight bounds in this range have been established, indicating the question's WRAM regime is settled.
